extraction.coverage: Full text read: all of _text/995e0e0b27e3.txt (lines 0-660, PDF pages 1551-1556, including abstract, introduction, related work, method, simulation results, conclusion and references). Metadata hint corrected: authors are Qingli Zeng and Farid Nait-Abdesselam (both University of Missouri-Kansas City); venue is IEEE ICC 2024; DOI is in the text. No Paul markup files existed (none), so paul_markup is empty. Content check: the paper contains no lobbying, legislators, elections, persuasion/turnout, allocation, text-measurement or social-network material. The only network-like element is distance-based neighbour interaction among drones. Those topics are therefore absent, not thin. The paper's own references to networks are to UAV communication surveys, not social networks.
extraction.research_question: Can drones trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning (Q-learning with function approximation) reproduce bird-flock behaviour (cohesion, alignment, separation, following) more adaptively than rule-based Boid models? The text states the aim as this comparison rather than as a formal question.
extraction.theory: Reynolds' Boid model (cohesion, separation, alignment) extended with a leader-follow rule and connectivity band, with reinforcement learning as the adaptive mechanism. Framework is an MDP tuple (S, A, P, R) solved by Q-learning, with linear Q-value approximation Q(s,a)=w·phi(s,a) and Bellman updates (Eqs. 2-6). Rewards are the sum of four terms (Eqs. 7-14).
extraction.data: No empirical data. Simulated drone swarm built in Python with Pygame. Unit: UAV (drone). Sample: N = 17 UAVs in the simulation parameters (Table I); training uses three designated UAVs (V1 leader on a predefined trajectory, V2 follower, V3 learner). Period: 3,500 simulation steps per method (Table II). Working area 600 x 800 units, maximum speed 4, distance thresholds d1=20, d2=40, d3=80 (Table I). Number of independent runs and random seeds are not reported.
extraction.method: Simulation comparison of two controllers: (a) Q-learning/MARL-trained drones with linear function approximation (learning rate initialised at alpha=0.1 and said to adapt across iterations; discount gamma=0.75) and (b) a rule-based Boid baseline. Reward weights from Table I: collision -20, connectivity +1, alignment with leader +5 (closer) and -1 (farther), cohesion +2. Sequential training: follower V2 learns to trail the leader at about 30 units; learner V3 learns to trail V1 while staying near V2 and avoiding collisions. Performance is reported as four counts or averages over the run: proximity advances, ideal-range tracking (20-40 units), near-collision events (within 20 units), and heading consistency (mean heading-angle difference, Eqs. 15-16). The rule-based baseline is not specified in the text beyond being a Boid-type rule model.
extraction.identification: None. The comparison is a single descriptive contrast of two controllers on one simulated scenario. No statistical test, confidence interval, replication, or ablation is reported.
extraction.scope: Population: simulated drones in a 2D Pygame environment (dimensionality is implied by the working-area dimensions but not stated). Institution: University of Missouri-Kansas City. Era: 2024. Results apply only to the single simulated scenario in Table I.

key_findings.finding: Abstract claims the MARL Boid surpasses rule-based models in cohesion, alignment and separation, and shows robustness to perturbations. Section IV reports only the Table II comparison; no perturbation experiment is reported in the text.
Both methods completed the task over the same horizon.
RL drones recorded more proximity advances than rule-based drones.
RL drones spent more instances within the ideal 20-40 unit range.
RL drones had far fewer near-collision events, which the authors read as improved safety.
key_findings.location: Table II and text, Section IV-B, p.1556

key_findings.finding: RL heading consistency is reported as better (lower average heading deviation, assuming the metric is a deviation, as defined on p.1556).

Conclusion: RL can minimise collisions, keep consistent headings and keep proximity, and may suit dynamic scenarios that hard-coded rules handle poorly. These are the authors' interpretations of the single comparison, not tested in the text.

measures: Distance between UAVs, d = ||u_i - u_j||_2 (Eq. 1)
Distance to flock centroid and change in it (Eqs. 8-10)
Distance to leader and change in it (Eqs. 11-12)
Heading angle folded to [0,180] and absolute heading difference, follower vs leader (Eqs. 15-16)
Proximity advances: count of steps in which distance to leader falls
Ideal range tracking: count of steps with distance between 20 and 40 units
Near-collision events: count of steps with distance under 20 units
Heading consistency: average heading deviation from leader (lower is better, per the definition)
limitations: Stated by the authors (Conclusion, p.1556): future research could explore more intricate behaviours, enhanced real-world applicability, and other advanced learning paradigms.

Not stated in the text but visible in it: a single simulated scenario; no reported seeds, replicates or variance; no description of the rule-based baseline's parameters; no perturbation experiment despite the robustness claim; the Table II counts are not normalised for the number of drones or area.

summary_md:
Zeng and Nait-Abdesselam (IEEE ICC 2024) train simulated drones with Q-learning and linear function approximation to reproduce Reynolds' Boid flocking rules: cohesion, alignment and separation, plus a leader-follow rule and a connectivity band. They compare this controller with an unspecified rule-based Boid baseline. The setup is one Pygame scenario with 17 UAVs and 3,500 steps. Training is sequential: one leader, one follower and one learner. Reward weights are fixed by hand (collision -20, alignment +5/-1, cohesion +2, connectivity +1).

Table II favours the RL controller on every count:
- proximity advances: 2,097 vs 1,976
- steps within the 20-40 unit ideal range: 3,176 vs 2,764
- near-collision events: 45 vs 108
- mean heading deviation: 14.3 vs 21.1

The evidence is thin. There is one scenario, with no seeds, replicates, variance or test. The baseline is never described. The counts are not normalised for swarm size. The abstract claims robustness to perturbations, but no perturbation experiment is reported.

For Paul's systems the paper is essentially out of scope. It contains no legislators, lobbying, money, text, elections or social-network structure. Its only network-like element is distance-based neighbour interaction among physical agents. The one thin link is methodological. It is another case of a learned policy beating a hand-set rule baseline, which is the kind of claim Paul's notes make when they expect GCOMB or contingency-aware RL to replace greedy allocation. On its own evidence the paper cannot support that expectation. A single uncontrolled, unreplicated comparison would not pass the project's single-look discipline, so it should be read only as an example of the claim type. It is not evidence for it. No component's assumptions, constants or code paths are tested, supported or contradicted by this work.

bearings.paper_claim: An RL controller (Q-learning, linear function approximation, alpha 0.1, gamma 0.75) beats a rule-based Boid baseline on one simulated drone scenario: near-collisions 45 vs 108 (-58%), ideal-range steps 3,176 vs 2,764 (+15%), heading deviation 14.3 vs 21.1, all over 3,500 steps with N = 17 UAVs. No seeds, replicates, variance or baseline specification are given.
bearings.paper_location: Table I (p.1555) and Table II with Section IV-B (p.1556)
bearings.system_side: The built optimizer uses deterministic CELF lazy greedy over per-member concave chunks ($500 steps, PMAX $10k cap, stance-gated members excluded). It has no learned policy. Paul's notes expect a learned policy (GCOMB) to replace greedy at scale.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as an analogy: a learned policy versus hand-set rules in a multi-agent setting. Nothing transfers to political allocation. The agents are physical drones, the reward is hand-specified geometry, and there is no budget, submodularity, money or legislator response. The evidence is one unreplicated simulation, so it cannot show that RL would outperform greedy anywhere, let alone on the cosponsor kernel.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Joint CU budget optimizer|Joint CU budget optimizer]]

gaps_exposed: None specific to the system. The paper's topic (drone swarm control) is absent from every component. The only general point is a reminder: if a learned allocation or seeding policy (GCOMB, contingency-aware RL) is ever built, its comparison with CELF greedy needs replicates, seeds and a fully specified baseline. This paper provides none of the three.
flags: Out of scope: the paper contains no lobbying, legislators, elections, persuasion, money, text-measurement or social-network material. Do not cite it as support for any Melange component.

Its RL-beats-rules claim rests on a single unreplicated simulation with no reported variance, and the robustness claim in the abstract has no experiment behind it. If it is ever cited for 'learned policies beat greedy/rule baselines', label the claim UNVERIFIED in line with the project's single-look and DE-062 standards.
Its distance-based neighbour interaction is not a social tie. It should not be read as support for neighbour-based stance imputation or cascade edges, whose co-movement test was null in this project.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation of this paper, and none of his component positions cite it. Its one point of contact is his expectation that a learned policy (GCOMB, Chen et al. 2021 contingency-aware RL) will eventually replace greedy allocation and seeding. The paper repeats the general claim that RL beats hand-set rules, but on evidence too thin to strengthen that expectation. It neither confirms nor dates any of his notes. The system as built (CELF greedy, the SGATE table) is unaffected.

related.why: Both use reinforcement learning to replace a hand-set rule policy. Chen et al. do it for seeding legislators-as-nodes under take-up uncertainty, which is the literature actually behind the SGATE seed gate. Zeng applies RL only to physical swarm control.

Same UAV application domain. Luo plans paths for single drones with D* Lite, while Zeng controls a swarm with RL. Both are engineering simulations relevant to Paul's pathfinding reading only by analogy.

Mismatch with the brief: the document is not an annotated literature review about Melange path-finding, social-network analysis, allocation, Moneyball, Mentat or Terrier. It is a status note on a sector-growth forecast collection (IBISWorld, Grand View Research, Statista, Swiss Re, Conning, credit unions, crypto, life insurance, autos). It names no Melange, Moneyball, Mentat or Terrier component, so system_links are empty throughout. The entries below cover the sources it cites, with Paul's status claims paraphrased, not the literature takeaways the brief described.

Document-level arguments and claims:
- The earlier collection was not exhaustive. It used a narrow immediately-preceding-year rule and should not have been presented as the maximum available data.
- The recheck found more evidence: a credit-union 2024 forecast (-1.13852850%) promoted to the main real-growth series, raising main usable values from 52 to 53; four auto forecasts for 2013-2016 from October 2011 reports; two combined auto forecasts for 2009-2010; four dated crypto multiyear outlooks; and one life-insurance forecast pair.

The main grid stays at 90 rows across five sectors. 55 IBISWorld numeric sector-year forecasts are collected, 53 meet strict checks, and the one-year crypto proxy stays separate.
- Scope discipline: older-vintage forecasts (2-5 years ahead) are preserved separately and do not establish the latest forecast before each spending year. Crypto multiyear outlooks may support a separate test of longer-horizon expectations but are not verified next-year forecasts. Life-insurance premium forecasts differ in scope and measure from life-and-annuity revenue and are kept apart.
- Qualification: the 2009-2010 auto values are qualified sensitivity inputs (medium-duty segment included for 2009; inferred common price scale for 2010).
- Status claim: "a verified partial collection with additional data and concrete remaining acquisition leads". Paul says the package is useful for analysis planning, and no claim of exhaustive collection is warranted.
- Stated gaps: (1) retired IBISWorld auto archives for 2012-2022 vintages could not be downloaded, and no verified matching pair was found publicly; (2) Conning life-annuity forecast archives (editions covering 2002-2015) not acquired; (3) Grand View Research's full licensed annual U.S. exchange-platform tables for 2017-2030 not obtained, only the public chart; (4) Swiss Re's December 2009 report URL was found but the PDF was not recovered.

summary_md:
This is the online appendix to *Personality on the Hill*, not the article. It has two tables of mean Big Five ratings of U.S. senators. Table A1 has about 129 rows from Senate insiders and APSA Congressional Fellows and feeds the main paper's Tables 2-5. Table A2 has about 126 rows from academics and is used only in the main paper's Table 1. Each row gives a rating count. The front note adds two facts that matter for anyone using the data. First, senators rated by only one coder appear in the tables but are excluded from every analysis in the main paper. Second, partisan composition is lopsided at the extremes. Democrats are 62% of the insiders' highest scorers and 65% of their lowest. In the academic table, 80% of high scores go to Democrats and 80% of low scores to Republicans. The appendix states no scale anchors, aggregation rule or era.

For Paul's system this is not background reading: it is the frozen external gold. `build_big5_senate_gold.py` turns the PDF into `big5_senate_expert_gold.json` (129 insider rows, 125 academic rows), and the trait validators score against it. So the appendix bears directly on how that gold is used:
- **Rating count.** The main validators keep single-coder rows. The paper drops them. Only some side probes stratify or weight by count.
- **Panel averaging.** The multitrait validator averages the two panels into one target, although the authors treat the academic panel as secondary.
- **Party.** Neither primary validator partials out party, while the academic panel's extremes are 80/80 party-sorted. That fits the recorded pattern that O passes only against academics and that lexical O reversed on the party check. That link is a hypothesis and stays UNVERIFIED.
- **Extraction.** The academic count of 125 against roughly 126 text rows, plus a malformed '4..33' cell, suggests the extractor may silently skip one row.

meta.title: Pitch Perfect: Vocal Pitch and the Emotional Intensity of Congressional Speech
meta.venue: American Political Science Review 113(4): 941-962 (received Oct 21, 2017; accepted July 1, 2019; published online Aug 23, 2019)

extraction.title: Pitch Perfect: Vocal Pitch and the Emotional Intensity of Congressional Speech
extraction.venue: American Political Science Review 113(4): 941-962 (received Oct 21, 2017; accepted July 1, 2019; published online Aug 23, 2019)
extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical; includes Supplemental Information referenced but not in the text file)
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (2,898 lines, printed pages 941-962, including all tables, footnotes 1-33 and the reference list) in six chunks; nothing skipped. Metadata hint confirmed from the text (title, authors, APSR 113(4), pp. 941-962, DOI all match). Paul's markup: no markup files were among the input set ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty and no highlights, underlines or sticky notes were read. Plain-text extraction drops figure images, so Figures 1-3 values come from the printed notes and prose. Table 3 group averages do not extract cleanly (Panel B pitch-difference column is garbled), so only the t-tests and text figures are relied on. The paper contains no lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation or vote-share-of-election analysis; the only election-related material is the literature review on voter responses to candidate pitch.
extraction.research_question: Do small within-speaker deviations in vocal pitch (mean F0 relative to a speaker's own baseline) measure legislators' emotional intensity on an issue? Test case: do female House members speak with higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, compared with (a) male MCs on the same topic and (b) their own speech on other topics? Secondary questions: does pitch track issue commitments (women's interest-group scores; party-owned issues), and do emotionally intense female speeches about women relate to male MCs' subsequent speech and voting (p. 941-942, 944, 951)?
extraction.theory: Emotional arousal tightens the vocal folds and raises pitch (Puts, Gaulin and Verdolini 2006; Owren and Bachorowski 2007; Mauss and Robinson 2009) (p. 942). Pitch is a measure of arousal/intensity, not valence (fn 1). Because pitch is hard to control, it sits low on the "leakage hierarchy" (Zuckerman and Driver 1985; Ekman et al. 1991; Kraut 1978), so it is a less strategic signal than topic choice, word choice or speech length (p. 942-944). Descriptive representation theory: female legislators have experience-based commitment to women's concerns (Reingold 1992; Mansbridge 1999), so their intensity should rise when speaking about women (p. 944-945). Signalling extension: when many women speak intensely about women, male colleagues attend and respond (Boyd, Epstein and Martin 2010; Mendelberg, Karpowitz and Oliphant 2014), with a possible backlash alternative (Kathlene 1994; Krook 2015) (p. 951, 957). Partisan extension: parties own issues and partisans speak with more intensity on owned issues (Petrocik 1996; Petrocik, Benoit and Hansen 2003) (p. 949-951).
extraction.data: Source: HouseLive (Office of the Clerk) video, audio and closed-caption text for all US House floor debates, 6,432 hours from 863 debates, 2009-01-06 to 2014-08-04 (p. 944). Unit of analysis: individual floor speech of at least 50 words; N = 74,158 speeches (p. 944). Speaker sex from GovTrack; race, seniority, DW-NOMINATE and party from GovTrack/Voteview; committee chair from Stewart and Woon (2016) (p. 946). Table 1 model N: 74,151 speeches and 619 MCs (Models 1.1-1.2); 71,198 speeches and 613 MCs (Models 1.3-1.4). Female-speech counts: 13,484 speeches by women (2,403 mention women, 17.82%); 60,667 by men (5,507 mention women, 9.08%) (p. 946). Women's own speech, male-on-female-day analysis: 50,235 speeches, 509 men (Table 5). Male pitch analysis: 49,914 speeches, 506 men (Table 6). Voting analysis: 21,920 observations, 485 men (Table 7). Interest groups: 24 women's groups via Project Vote Smart, averaged per MC (p. 948). Women's bills: Volden, Wiseman and Wittmer (2018); CQ "Bills to Watch" count (p. 952). Closed captions reported ~95% accurate by the vendor; authors' transcription of 100 speeches matched (fn 11).
extraction.method: Pitch: mean fundamental frequency per speech extracted with Praat (Boersma 1993 algorithm; male floor 75 Hz, ceiling 300 Hz; female range 100-500 Hz), then z-scored within speaker so units are SD above/below each MC's baseline (p. 945-946; alternative Praat windows in SI S22-S30). Topic: binary indicator for any term in Pearson and Dancey (2011b) women dictionary; alternatives are word-share and a 30-topic structural topic model (STM) (p. 945-946). Models: multilevel logit for "Women mentioned" (Models 1.1-1.2, 5.1-5.2) and multilevel linear regression for standardized pitch with random intercepts per MC (Models 1.3-1.4, 4.x, 6.x); outcome models for Table 5, 6, 7 are multilevel logit/linear with day-level Female Speeches, Female Pitch and interactions (p. 946-956). Descriptive comparisons: Welch-type t-tests across speakers and groups (Table 2; Table 3 top-25 vs bottom-25 female MCs by pitch difference; t = 2.59, df = 48). Partisan issue test: Table 4 interaction of party with party-owned STM topics. Male voting outcome: proportion of votes cast with female speakers, standardized against each male MC's prior co-voting rate (p. 955-956). Predicted values from Models 5.2, 6.1 and 7.2 at female pitch +/-2 SD (p. 953-956).
extraction.identification: None causal. The paper states the design is observational and that "legislators' speeches on women simply cannot be randomly assigned" (p. 957). Within-speaker z-scoring removes stable speaker-level pitch differences (including sex differences in baseline pitch), random intercepts absorb unobserved MC heterogeneity, and a rich control set is used (race, seniority, chair, DW-NOMINATE, party, one-minute speech, duration, election year). Placebo tests and dyadic models are in SI S55-S62. Male-response models restrict to men who spoke on the same legislative day as women's speeches and add agenda controls (Women's bills, CQ bills). The volume-times-pitch interaction is the key test. Robustness: results unchanged under alternative DV operationalizations (word share, STM) (p. 946), re-estimated without observations beyond +/-2 SD (fn 28, p. 953), and different Praat pitch windows (p. 945-946).
extraction.scope: Population: all US House floor speeches of at least 50 words during the 111th-113th Congresses (Jan 2009 to Aug 2014), roughly 77-81 women in the House in that span (p. 956). Institution: US House floor only (not the Senate, committees, or state legislatures, which the authors name as future audio sources, p. 958). Era: 2009-2014. Speeches are natural floor speech, not acted or induced emotion (p. 944). The authors explicitly do not claim general causal effects of women's speech on male behavior (p. 957).
measures: Standardized mean F0 (vocal pitch) per speech, in SD above/below speaker baseline (Praat; Titze 2000 F0 framework)
Raw mean F0 in Hz (Table 2 and footnote 15)
Women-mention dictionary indicator (Pearson and Dancey 2011b), with word-share and STM alternatives
Female (GovTrack sex)
Party, DW-NOMINATE, seniority, committee chair, race, one-minute speech, speech duration, election year
Pitch difference: mean Hz when mentioning women minus not mentioning (Table 3)
Women's interest-group scores: average of 24 Project Vote Smart scorecards
Women's bills introduced (Volden, Wiseman and Wittmer 2018) and CQ Bills to Watch (count per legislative day)
Party-owned issue topics from a 30-topic STM (9 Democratic-owned, 9 Republican-owned categories)
Female Speeches (count per day of women's speeches mentioning women) and Female Pitch (their average standardized pitch)
Male co-voting with female speakers, standardized against each male MC's prior co-voting (Voteview votes)

key_findings.finding: Women are more likely than men to reference women in floor speeches.
key_findings.numbers: 17.82% of female speeches (2,403/13,484) vs 9.08% of male speeches (5,507/60,667); predicted probability 0.17 vs 0.08 (2.13 times). Holds with controls (Model 1.2).

key_findings.finding: Female MCs speak at higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, and male MCs do not.
key_findings.numbers: Female x 'Women mentioned' = 0.090 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) without controls and 0.112 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) with controls. Female MCs: +0.09 SD when referencing women, about five times the male change of +0.02 SD. Male pitch unchanged (t = 0.02, df 58,281). Democratic women t = 3.12; Republican women t = 2.81.

key_findings.finding: Raw pitch levels: female MCs' pitch rises on speeches mentioning women; male pitch is flat.
key_findings.numbers: Female MCs: 206.01 Hz when mentioning women vs 203.27 Hz otherwise. Male MCs: 151.50 Hz vs 151.49 Hz. Republican women 207.02 Hz vs Democratic women 205.68 Hz when mentioning women (not significantly different, fn 15).

key_findings.finding: Among female MCs, the most emotionally intense on women's issues have higher women's interest-group scores.
key_findings.numbers: Top 25 vs bottom 25 female MCs by pitch difference: difference in Vote Smart scores t = 2.59, df = 48, p < 0.02. Democratic women only: t = 2.83, df = 39, p <= 0.01. Republican women: t = 0.14, df = 7, not significant (small N). Table 3 group averages are not reliably extracted and are not relied on.

key_findings.finding: Partisans speak with higher pitch on their party-owned issues and lower pitch on the opposing party's issues.
key_findings.numbers: Democrat x Democratic-owned issues = 0.328 (Model 4.1) and 0.288 (Model 4.2), both p<0.01. Republican x Republican-owned issues = 0.380 (Model 4.3) and 0.355 (Model 4.4), both p<0.01. Democrats use 9.02% more words on Democratic-owned topics; Republicans use 17.21% more on Republican-owned topics (t = 18.43 and 30.51). Topic shares capture under 8% of words per speech on average.

key_findings.finding: Male MCs mention women more often on days with more female speeches on women, and more so when female pitch is high in the interaction model.
key_findings.numbers: Table 5 Model 5.2: Female speeches = 0.060 (SE 0.003); Female speeches x Female pitch = 0.011 (p<0.05). Figure 1 (Female pitch +2 SD): going from 0 to 43 female speeches raises P(male mention of women) from 0.05 to 0.56. From 6 to 11 speeches (1 SD either side of mean): 0.07 to 0.10. Model 5.1 interaction is not significant at 0.05.

key_findings.finding: Male MCs' pitch on women rises with the volume and intensity of female speeches on women.
key_findings.numbers: Three-way interaction (Women mentioned x Female speeches x Female pitch) = 0.016 (SE 0.005, p<0.01). At Female pitch +2 SD, raising female speeches from 6 to 11 moves male pitch on women from 0.17 SD to 0.26 SD; from 0 to 43 moves it from 0.12 SD to 1.79 SD.

key_findings.finding: Male co-voting with female speakers rises with the volume and intensity of women's speeches; no backlash detected.
key_findings.numbers: Female speeches x Female pitch = 0.015 (Model 7.1, p<0.01) and 0.012 (Model 7.2, SE 0.002, p<0.01). At Female pitch +2 SD, the standardized co-voting rate rises from -0.23 SD to +0.53 SD as female speeches go from 0 to 43 (p. 956). Authors read this as no evidence of male backlash (p. 957).

key_findings.finding: The maximum observed volume of female speeches on women is large relative to the chamber.
key_findings.numbers: 43 female speeches on women on one day = 56% of the 77-81 women in the 111th-113th Congresses.

key_findings.finding: Results are robust to alternative outcome measures and to trimming extreme pitch values.
key_findings.location: p. 946 (alternative DVs); fn 28, p. 953 (+/-2 SD trim); SI S30-S36, S66-S69
key_findings.numbers: Word-share and STM operationalizations of women-topic give identical substantive results. Trimming pitch beyond +/-2 SD is 'generally robust' (no numbers reported in text).

limitations: Observational design; the authors say they do not claim causal effects of female MCs' intense speech on male behavior, and that alternative explanations cannot be ruled out (p. 957).
Male response is not zero at low female participation: at few female speeches the effect is absent or negative, so the signalling story is conditional on volume (p. 957).
Backlash is examined only with one voting measure and cannot be ruled out in other outcomes; votes may come before or after speeches because the data have no time stamps (fn 31, p. 955-956).
Pitch-based intensity is an arousal measure, not valence; a single pitch number cannot say whether a speaker is enthusiastic or angry (fn 1, p. 942).
Mean F0 per speech is a coarse measure; other factors (question intonation, duration) also move mean pitch, though controls are included (fn 8, p. 945; p. 958-959).
Women-topic is a coarse dictionary indicator; alternatives used as robustness checks (p. 945-946).
Effect size is small: 0.09 SD for female MCs on women's topics, which the authors concede is 'slight' and likely below conscious control (p. 947).
Confidence and expertise could explain some intensity; the paper does not separate them, and male MCs with the most women's bills did not show the same pattern (fn 19, p. 948).

Republican-owned and Republican-women effects are weaker or not significant in some specifications, partly due to small N of Republican women (p. 948-949; fn 17; t = 0.14 with df = 7 for Republican women in Table 3 comparison).

summary_md:
Dietrich, Hayes and O'Brien use 74,158 US House floor speeches from 2009 to 2014, each at least 50 words, taken from Clerk HouseLive audio. They measure each speech's mean vocal pitch (F0, extracted with Praat) and z-score it against the speaker's own baseline. They argue this is a hard-to-fake measure of arousal. It tracks intensity, not valence (footnote 1). Female members speak about 0.09 to 0.11 SD above their baseline when they mention women, while male members do not change (Table 1). Partisans speak about 0.29 to 0.38 SD higher on topics their party owns (Table 4). On days when many women speak with high pitch about women, male members mention women more, raise their own pitch on the topic, and co-vote more with the women speakers (Tables 5-7). These response results are observational, and the authors say they are not causal (p. 957).

The system has already built this method. `fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:209-254` cites the paper by name and computes `pitch_deviation_from_speaker_baseline_z` and `topic_emotional_intensity`. The two differ in three ways. The paper relies on a cross-speaker contrast (female versus male, times topic) and roughly 120 speeches per speaker. The system reports a per-speaker topic mean with no comparison group. Its floors are 5 speech units per member, 2 topics, and 2 units per topic (`fec/audio_rules.py:20-22`). Effects of 0.1 to 0.4 SD cannot be detected at those floors. With only two topics, the sign of each topic's deviation is fixed by construction. The paper also measures in one floor venue with one channel. The system's baseline is pooled across interview programs and channels. The paper supports the system's existing rules: absolute F0 stays out of personality scores, and audio stays display-only. It also points to a better identity source: Clerk floor video, where the chamber has already identified the speaker.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotional intensity is measured as each speech's mean F0 z-scored against the speaker's own baseline, in SD units. Detecting the effect needed about 120 speeches per member on average (74,151 speeches from 619 members). The female × women-mentioned effect is 0.090 SD (SE 0.027) without controls and 0.112 SD with controls. The party-owned-issue effect is 0.29-0.38 SD. The authors call the 0.09 SD effect 'slight'.
bearings.system_side: The candidate v2 descriptor converts eGeMAPS semitones to Hz and cites Dietrich, Hayes & O'Brien in a code comment. It z-scores each speech unit against the member's mean and SD and reports `topic_emotional_intensity` as the mean deviation per topic. Required floors: at least 5 speech units per member, at least 2 topics, and at least 2 units per reported topic. No comparison group is used. The output is a candidate artifact that nothing consumes (status CANDIDATE_CONSUMED_BY_NOTHING_AWAITING_USER_RATIFICATION), and the v2 artifact holds 0 accepted clips.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transform (within-speaker z of mean F0) carries over directly. The inference does not. Dietrich's evidence is a difference-in-differences across speakers over thousands of speeches. A single member's topic mean from 2-5 units has an SE of roughly 0.45-0.7 SD, larger than every effect the paper reports. With exactly 2 topics, the two topic deviations must have opposite signs by construction (their unit-weighted sum is zero). The paper used floor speech from one Clerk source. The system uses on-air interviews across outlets and channels, which the paper never tested.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: Mean F0 also moves with question intonation, speech duration and speech type (one-minute speeches), so the paper adds these as controls. The baseline comes from one venue (House floor, HouseLive). Pitch measures arousal, not valence.
bearings.system_side: The baseline is pooled across all accepted units from at least 2 programs and 2 sources. Channel (studio, remote or telephone) is recorded in the brain as uncontrolled. Neither the per-member z nor the WJ subject_effects centering controls for duration or questions. The Washington Journal subject_effects shown on the desk report per-member topic pitch shifts from as few as 2 reactions.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies wherever the system compares a member's pitch across topics. Channel and venue differences shift F0 by more than the paper's 0.1 SD effects, so a topic that appears mostly on one program will pick up that program's offset. The 'meaning' string calls the output 'relative emotional intensity', which is safe only as arousal. It must never be read as anger or enthusiasm.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: Raw F0 differs mostly by sex (female 203-206 Hz vs male about 151 Hz, Table 2). The intensity signal is the deviation from each speaker's own baseline, so stable between-speaker pitch differences carry no intensity information. The measure is a topic-level state, not a trait.
bearings.system_side: The output contract sets 'absolute_f0_enters_personality': False and 'audio_may_modify_big_five': False. It explicitly excludes 'absolute F0 or inferred gender as a personality input'. The brain records that pitch_variability_raw is sex-confounded (r = -0.266) and that the audio-prosody N pilot MISSed at N = 90.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The support is direct. The paper's design removes between-speaker level by construction, so it offers no evidence that pitch measures a between-member disposition such as N. This agrees with the closed audio-N route and the display-only ruling.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: The corpus is the Office of the Clerk's HouseLive video, audio and closed captions, 6,432 hours across 863 debates, where the chamber has already attributed each speech to a member. The vendor reports captions as about 95% accurate, and the authors' check of 100 speeches matched.
bearings.system_side: Clips are kept when Haiku 4.5 reads them from YouTube auto-captions as SOLO_TARGET and MATCH or NEUTRAL. The brain records that about 33.7% of kept clips rest on evidence with no identifying content. Search-fetched floor audio had about 38% contamination before the 2026-07-09 fix.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only to House floor audio, and only from 2009 onward, where Clerk video carries speaker identification. It would not cover interviews, Sunday shows, Senate audio or hearings. It would replace the guessed identity on floor clips with the chamber's own record, but it does not touch the interview corpus where the identity gap is largest.

bearings.paper_claim: Text features such as topic choice, word choice and length sit high on the leakage hierarchy, so speakers control them strategically. Vocal pitch largely lies beyond the speaker's control. The paper offers audio as a measure of intensity that text cannot give.
bearings.system_side: Press intensity is |LSD net| / words or (pos+neg)/words on member press releases. The press pillar multiplies stance sign by this 'heat'. The brain note treats it as how heated a release is.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a theoretical argument, not a test of LSD. The paper never compares dictionary tone with pitch. Press releases are drafted by staff, so they are even more strategic than floor speech. LSD intensity therefore measures crafted rhetorical tone, not felt intensity, and should be labelled that way. It does not invalidate the tone term as a measure of messaging emphasis.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity|Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity]]

bearings.paper_claim: Male MCs' same-day co-voting with female speakers rises with Female speeches × Female pitch: 0.015 (Model 7.1) and 0.012 (Model 7.2, SE 0.002). At +2 SD pitch the standardized co-voting rate moves from -0.23 to +0.53 SD as speeches go from 0 to 43. The male response is absent or negative at low volume.
bearings.system_side: Linear-threshold priming sums neighbour pressure against a tier threshold. The cue weight depends only on bipartisanship (sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v)), with no term for the intensity of the signal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The result is observational and gender-specific (women's issues, 2009-2014). It concerns floor co-voting within a day, which has no time stamps, so votes may come before the speeches. It is not about cosponsorship. The pattern of no response at low volume and a response at high volume is compatible with threshold adoption, but it does not test it. It should not be used to set any engine constant.

gaps_exposed: No comparison group. The paper's evidence is a cross-speaker contrast (female vs male, times topic), but topic_emotional_intensity reports one member's topic mean with nothing to compare it against (b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:237-249).

Power. The floors are 5 units per member, 2 topics and 2 units per topic (audio_rules.py:20-22). At those floors the SE of a topic mean is roughly 0.45-0.7 SD, while the paper's effects are 0.09-0.38 SD and needed about 120 speeches per member. No minimum detectable effect is reported anywhere.

The sign is fixed by construction when a member has 2 topics. The brain records a within-member permutation-null fix (sign_informative, commit 4193f0140 on the unmerged speech-recognition branch), but the live b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py has no null or sign_informative field. UNVERIFIED drift between brain and live tree.

No controls for question intonation, speech duration or speech type, and no venue or channel term, in either the per-member z or the WJ subject_effects (build_descriptive_speech.py:2491-2531). The paper treats these as confounds of mean F0.
The floor-speech audio does not use Clerk HouseLive, where the chamber has already attributed each speech to a member. The system instead verifies identity from captions with an LLM.
No issue-ownership check. The paper's party-owned-topic pitch effect (0.29-0.38 SD) gives a ready external sanity check for any topic-pitch descriptor, and the system has not run it.
flags: The desk shows per-member topic pitch shifts from as few as 2 WJ reactions (build_descriptive_speech.py:2521; make_member_desk_00.tpl:1280). The window and count are shown, but at that n the values are noise relative to the paper's effect sizes. Treat them as UNVERIFIED descriptive output, never as an intensity finding.

The brain says topic_emotional_intensity was fixed with a permutation null, but the live candidate file lacks it. This is a committed-vs-live discrepancy, and per DE-062 it stays UNVERIFIED until a second check of the branch.

The paper's male-response results (Tables 5-7) are observational and gender-specific (authors, p. 957). Any import into cascade or threshold constants would be unvalidated. Do not describe them as influence probabilities.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025. The paper does not touch cosponsorship edges, edge normalization or LDA.
paul_alignment: Paul lists this paper as on disk without annotation, under his interest in non-textual channels for the prosody component. The paper confirms that pitch can carry a real signal, but only as a within-speaker state (arousal by topic), only with large samples, and only through cross-speaker contrasts. That matches the system's ruling that audio is display-only and never feeds the Big Five scores (b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:358). His note is out of date in one way: the method has already been transplanted, and the code cites the paper by name at b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:210. The open question is no longer whether to use pitch. It is whether the implementation meets the paper's sample and comparison requirements, and at current floors it does not. His margin note on Joo ('Monitoring tool?') concerns a different Dietrich paper, on video and aisle crossing, not this one.

related.why: Covers the general pitfalls of audio as political data (alignment, feature choice, classifiers) that this paper's single-venue pitch design sidesteps. Together they inform whether the system's cross-venue interview baseline is defensible.

Both measure elites from speech. Ramey reads traits from words, while Dietrich argues words are strategic and pitch less so. This is the text-versus-voice tension behind the lexical Big Five and audio lanes.
The brain uses Salam to sex-condition prosody features. Dietrich's within-speaker z is the alternative fix for the same sex confound in F0.

Marrero asks whether voice carries trait (personality) information. Dietrich's design deliberately strips between-speaker level and treats pitch as a topic-level state, which argues against reading traits from F0.
Joo's piece on non-text political data is where Paul's margin note about Dietrich's video work sits. This paper is the audio counterpart in that line of work.

backlinks.why: It measures the emotional intensity of congressional speech through vocal pitch rather than emotion-word counts, which this review shows are sparse at under 5% of words.
Vocal pitch in congressional speech measures emotional intensity, not trait. It is the political-domain counterpart to Rubio's lab interview setting.
